summary:
The national framework applies in Maharashtra as it does across India. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026; the bill amends the 2019 law, removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex people, and makes medical certification a condition of recognition. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. The BBC reports that the bill was approved by both houses of Parliament and awaits presidential assent, and that it reverses the Supreme Court of India's 2014 ruling on third gender and self-determination.

Human Rights Watch, in a news release of 26 March 2026, calls the amendment a huge setback. It objects to the new offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender, provisions it describes as reminiscent of colonial-era laws that punished transgender people for presenting dressed as women.

Identification documents are a narrow channel. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, while only about 32,500 hold the identity cards on which access to social security depends.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court of India in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical examination by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.

Judicial protection machinery exists alongside that record. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Care access has a national floor. The Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community.
tangentialFactors:
The amendment is contested in terms that shape how a visitor reads official statements. Lawyer N Kavitha Rameshwar called the medical-certification requirement an "attack on the privacy and dignity of the individual", while the government argues that the narrower definition targets those facing "extreme and oppressive" discrimination and prevents exploitation and trafficking. Critics warned that the narrower definition could exclude many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people from welfare benefits.

Intersex visitors and intersex minors travelling with families face a distinct exposure. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.

In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries, which bears on how a couple handles money and next-of-kin designation while in India.
localsOnly:
Facilities and welfare delivery are largely set at state level, and Maharashtra is one of the states that run this machinery. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha operate transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras.

Residents seeking legal recognition must now satisfy the medical certification the 2026 amendment makes a condition of recognition, and identity cards remain the gateway to social security; roughly 32,500 people hold them against a census count of 487,803 transgender persons.

Transition-related healthcare for residents sits under the Ayushman Bharat scheme, expanded in April 2024 to all members of the transgender community.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the amendment bill was outstanding in the source material, which records approval by both houses of Parliament; the assent stage and any commencement date are unresolved here.

No source in the inventory states how the amended recognition scheme is administered in Maharashtra, which authority issues recognition or identity cards at state level, or whether the Maharashtra transgender welfare board continues to register people who fall outside the new categories. These points are not sourced.

Whether Maharashtra has its own prohibition on conversion therapy, or applies the directions issued by the Madras High Court in S. Sushma, is not addressed by the sources.

The police-conduct evidence in the inventory (the United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note, the June 2024 victim interviews, the airport and railway incidents in Chennai, Kolkata and Assam) is national or drawn from other states. No Maharashtra-specific record of police treatment of trans detainees is sourced here.

Whether the welfare board benefits available to Maharashtra residents survive the narrowing of legal recognition under the 2026 amendment is unresolved in the source inventory.
